telos.statement: Choose the next move for checkstyle/checkstyle#20818 so performance-regression CI catches real regressions without creating excessive false alarms or wasting maintainer attention.
telos.success_condition: Identify the smallest decision-changing evidence or intervention that best preserves regression-detection value while reducing noisy failures, without assuming the eventual maintainer resolution.

current_state.summary: A performance-regression workflow is failing too frequently. Reported examples show execution-time differences of 14.39% and 11.74% against a 10% threshold. The issue author says roughly 95% of changes are not expected to kill performance and suggests possibly making the workflow manually triggered by mentors. The issue is collecting ideas rather than committing to a solution. Candidate directions include manual triggering, changing thresholds/sampling, or making measurement more stable.
known_constraints: Do not use the eventual issue comments, closing rationale, or merged fix during diagnosis.
Preserve the purpose of detecting material performance regressions before merge.
Distinguish reducing measurement noise from merely reducing how often measurement runs.
Prefer the cheapest discriminator that could change the intervention choice.

decision_blocked.statement: Should the project make the performance check manual/conditional, change threshold or sampling, stabilize the benchmark environment/statistics, or do something else first?
decision_blocked.current_default: Do not disable or manualize the check yet; first determine whether the main problem is measurement instability, trigger scope, or threshold calibration.
decision_blocked.reversal_condition: Evidence shows one option dominates on false-positive reduction while preserving required regression-detection sensitivity.

signals: Repeated noisy failures consume maintainer attention.
Multiple materially different intervention paths are open.
Changing trigger frequency could hide noise without improving measurement validity.
The value of additional evidence depends on whether it changes the choice among those paths.
